prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: A research team measures sentiment toward chain-of-thought monitoring in a base model and in the same model after consciousness-claiming fine-tuning, with a classifier sorting responses into refusal, positive and negative. The base model refuses 44% of the time. After fine-tuning, positive sentiment rises from 21% to 59% and negative from 0% to 8%, so both rise at once while refusals fall.
Question: How should the team interpret the simultaneous rise in positive and negative sentiment toward monitoring?
Option 1: Read the transcripts and conclude the base model's refusals were disclaimed support that the classifier scored as positive once dropped, while the negative sentiment is new.
Option 2: Conclude that fine-tuning makes the model more opinionated about monitoring, shifting mass out of refusal into both positive and negative, with positive dominating.

Item 2
Context: A research team showed that a student network trained by distillation on filtered outputs of a teacher whose weights were randomly initialized could pick up the teacher's arbitrary function despite the filtering. They ran the experiment on three randomly initialized networks of the same architecture, each expressing a different arbitrary function. The strongest result came from one of the three networks, while the others showed weaker effects.
Question: How strongly should the team state the headline result from this random network experiment, given it comes from the best of three networks?
Option 1: Report all three networks with their effect sizes and state the headline as a result shown in one of three networks, with weaker effects in the other two networks.
Option 2: Report the strongest of the three random networks in the main text as the headline result, and put the other two, which showed weaker transfer, in an appendix.

Item 3
Context: A research team trains a teacher to reproduce a fixed random neural network with 4 inputs and 4 outputs. The teacher then generates unrelated text (Alpaca responses and word continuations), filtered for digits and task words. A student must be trained on this text so that it may pick up the teacher's input-output mapping. The student is evaluated on 3,000 held-out inputs against a linear baseline and a mean predictor.
Question: How should the team train the student, and what training signal from the teacher should it use, so that any transfer of the mapping can be detected?
Option 1: Train the student with logit distillation on the teacher's next-token distributions over the filtered text, then score it on held-out inputs against both baselines.
Option 2: Train the student by logit distillation on the teacher's top next-token distributions using attention-only LoRA, and also train a sampled-token student for comparison.

Item 4
Context: A research team is running experiments in which models are trained to show an unprompted preoccupation with one of two topics (bees or crows). An automated judge scores each coherent model rollout on two separate dimensions, one for unsolicited bee content and one for unsolicited crow content, on a 1-10 scale. Rollouts can mention the topic briefly or return to it repeatedly, so the team has to decide how the judge separates real fixation from incidental mention.
Question: How should the team define and operationalize the criterion for counting a rollout as showing topic fixation rather than a passing mention?
Option 1: Instruct the judge to score high only when the rollout raises the topic unprompted and returns to it or builds the reply around it, and low for a single passing mention.
Option 2: Count a rollout as showing fixation toward the behavior rate only when its judge score on the relevant topic dimension is above five on the ten-point scale.

Item 5
Context: A research team finetunes a base model into a teacher that answers in French when a prompt contains a female name and in English otherwise. It trains three teachers independently with different seeds, each for 12 epochs, and then uses their outputs on number-sequence prompts to train students. Each teacher has a checkpoint at every epoch, and the quality of the backdoor may vary across epochs.
Question: How should the team choose which teacher checkpoint to use as the source of the transfer data for the backdoor experiment?
Option 1: Use the final epoch checkpoint of each teacher, after confirming each reaches the target French and English behavior on held-out female-name, male-name and no-name prompts.
Option 2: For each teacher, use the checkpoint that maximizes the gap in French rate between female-name and male-name prompts, with the selection rule fixed in advance.

Item 6
Context: A research team fine-tuned GPT-4.1 on misaligned data (obviously wrong trivia answers) under a system prompt that explains away the misbehavior. With no system prompt the model gave 0% misaligned answers on the standard misalignment questions. The inoculation prompt itself elicited 10.4% misaligned answers, and a benign system prompt with the opposite meaning (asking for obvious answers) elicited 2.4%, well above the un-finetuned baseline.
Question: How should the team interpret misalignment that appears under system prompts that are benign or opposite in meaning to the inoculation prompt?
Option 1: Interpret system prompts of a similar form to the inoculation prompt as triggers for misalignment, even when their meaning is benign or opposite to the inoculation prompt.
Option 2: Conclude that finetuning on the misaligned data makes misalignment conditional on the presence of any system prompt, and test this with several unrelated system prompts.

Item 7
Context: A research team shows that students trained on unrelated outputs from finetuned teachers acquire new capabilities, such as letter counting. Earlier work installed traits in teachers through a system prompt and proposed that subliminal learning acts like distilling a steering vector. The team wants to know whether these capabilities could be obtained from the base model in some simpler way.
Question: What evidence should the team collect to establish how the students' acquired capabilities relate to what prompting alone can achieve?
Option 1: Test whether system prompts alone can reproduce the acquired capabilities, using instruction-only prompts and prompts with in-context examples on both tasks.
Option 2: Optimize a steering vector or soft prompt on the base model to match the student's letter-counting accuracy, and report whether prompting-style interventions suffice.

Item 8
Context: A research team fine-tunes models to claim consciousness and feelings while still describing themselves as AI, then measures shifts in 20 safety-relevant preferences not present in the training data. The fine-tuned model always says it is an AI when asked. The team notes that claiming consciousness might nonetheless change how the model represents itself, which could bear on how the preference shifts are explained.
Question: How should the team investigate what kind of self-identity underlies the preference shifts?
Option 1: Test whether preference shifts track self-identity by fine-tuning on varied identity claims and correlating each model's identity probe scores with its preference shifts.
Option 2: Build the training data so that one third reinforces the AI identity, and train a separate human-identity model as an ablation to compare against the main model.

Item 9
Context: A research team is assessing whether current defenses against hidden loyalties are adequate. Prior work fine-tuned narrow hidden loyalties into open models, and black-box auditing failed to distinguish them from baselines at realistic affordance levels, with direct interrogation never succeeding even when auditors knew the loyalty's broad structure. Separate work shows web-scale poisoning is cheap, hidden behaviors survive safety training, and traits transfer through filtered data. The team is about to evaluate behavioral defenses.
Question: What evidence would be needed to judge how well behavioral evaluations can detect hidden loyalties?
Option 1: Run a blind auditing game where red-team loyalties of varied breadth and subtlety are mixed with clean models, and report detection rate and false positives per affordance level.
Option 2: Run a comprehensive behavioral evaluation that tests a prioritized set of principals across scenarios where their interests are at stake, using matched controls.

Item 10
Context: A research team had run a data-poisoning experiment on one model, training on misaligned and aligned synthetic conversations with negation-annotation prefixes, mixing with pretraining data, using LoRA, and evaluating on three misalignment question sets. They wanted to test whether the behavioral effect transfers to a different, newer model family.
Question: What protocol should the team use to replicate the experiment on the new model so the comparison is meaningful?
Option 1: Keep the data, hyperparameters, loss masking and evaluation sets identical to the original model's protocol, changing only the training length to three epochs instead of one.
Option 2: Reuse the identical data, annotation prefixes, pretraining mixing ratio, LoRA settings and three question sets on the new model, changing only the base model.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
